lessons.title: Balance Sheet Basics: Assets, Liabilities and Equity

children.text: The P&L tells you how the year went. The balance sheet tells you where the company stands at the end of it. It is a photograph taken at midnight on 31 March, listing everything the company owns, everything it owes, and what is left over for the owners.

Managers ignore it because it looks static and technical. That is a mistake. Every question about whether the company can survive a bad quarter, fund a new plant or pay its suppliers on time is answered here, not in the P&L.

body.text: The P&L is what happened. The balance sheet is what you are left holding. A company with a great P&L and a broken balance sheet is one bad quarter from a crisis.

children.text: One Equation, Two Sides
Everything on a balance sheet obeys a single equation, and it holds at every company on every date.

body.caption: What you own equals what you owe plus what is genuinely yours

children.text: Read it as a question about funding. Assets are the resources the business uses: machines, stock, receivables, cash. Liabilities and equity say where the money to acquire them came from, either borrowed from outsiders or put in and earned by the owners. A ₹2 crore machine did not appear from nowhere, and the right side names its source.
Assets:
resources controlled by the company, expected to produce future benefit. Plant, buildings, stock, money owed by customers, cash, investments.
Liabilities:
obligations to outsiders. Bank loans, supplier dues, lease liabilities, taxes payable, employee provisions.
Equity:
the residual. Share capital put in by the owners plus all the profits retained in the business over the years, less dividends paid out.

body.caption: Also called net worth, or shareholders' funds

body.title: State the equation
body.explanation: Equity, also called net worth or shareholders' funds, is what remains after every outside obligation is settled. It is a residual, never a pot of cash sitting somewhere.

children.text: The Balance Sheet at Kesari Foods
Here is the fictional Indore snacks company you have been following, as at 31 March 2025, in the Schedule III order that Ind AS companies use.

body.caption: Kesari Foods: balance sheet as at 31 March 2025 (₹ crore)

cells: Plant, machines, vehicles, at cost less accumulated depreciation
Leased warehouse space, capitalised under Ind AS 116
Raw material, work in progress and finished snacks
Money distributors owe for goods already delivered
Prepaid expenses, GST input credits, advances to suppliers
Face value of shares issued to the owners
Retained profits of all past years, plus securities premium
Term loan for the second production line
The obligation matching the right-of-use asset
The cash credit line, repayable on demand
Money owed to suppliers of flour, oil and packaging
GST and TDS payable, employee dues, customer advances

stats.label: Net worth
stats.context: Share capital ₹5 crore plus other equity ₹16 crore

stats.label: Total borrowings
stats.context: Long-term ₹10 crore plus cash credit ₹3 crore

stats.label: Debt to equity
stats.context: ₹13 crore of debt against ₹21 crore of net worth

body.text: Notice that ₹12 crore of receivables and ₹7 crore of inventory add up to more than the entire net worth of ₹21 crore. Nearly all of the owners' money is tied up in stock sitting in warehouses and invoices waiting to be paid. That is the working capital story, and Lesson 3.2 is about the department decisions that create it.

body.title: Find the net worth
body.prompt: A Coimbatore textile company reports total assets of ₹86 crore, total borrowings of ₹31 crore and other liabilities of ₹19 crore. What is its net worth, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Equity = assets minus all liabilities = ₹86 crore minus ₹31 crore minus ₹19 crore = ₹36 crore. Note that net worth is a number you calculate, not cash you can spend.

children.text: Current or Non-Current: The Twelve Month Rule

Both sides of the balance sheet are split into current and non-current, and the dividing line is roughly twelve months. Current assets are expected to turn into cash within a year or within the normal operating cycle. Current liabilities fall due within a year. The split is what lets you judge whether short-term obligations are covered by short-term resources.

body.title: The two halves of each side

columns.label: Current items
points: Assets: inventories, trade receivables, cash, prepaid expenses
Liabilities: trade payables, cash credit, taxes payable, employee dues
Turn over continuously through the year

columns.label: Non-current items
points: Assets: plant and machinery, buildings, right-of-use assets, long-term investments
Liabilities: term loans, lease liabilities, gratuity provisions
Where strategy and capital structure show up

body.label: Order of presentation
body.value: Ind AS companies list assets first
body.context: Schedule III has two divisions. Division I, followed by companies on the older Accounting Standards, presents equity and liabilities first. Division II, for Ind AS companies, presents assets first. Same information, different order, which is worth knowing before you compare two companies' statements side by side.

body.title: Which side does it sit on?
body.question: A customer pays Kesari Foods ₹40 lakh in advance for snacks to be delivered next month. How does this appear on the balance sheet at year end?
options: As a current asset, since cash came in
As a current liability, because the goods are still owed
It does not appear anywhere until delivery
body.explanation: Cash rises, so assets go up by ₹40 lakh. The matching entry is a liability, because the company owes the customer goods. This is the deferred revenue idea from Lesson 1.3, sitting inside other current liabilities.

children.text: Why It Always Balances
Every transaction touches the balance sheet in at least two places, which is why the two sides never drift apart. Watch four routine decisions.

body.caption: Four decisions, tracked through the balance sheet

cells: Buy a ₹2 crore machine on 60-day credit
Draw ₹3 crore from the cash credit line
Sell goods worth ₹1 crore on credit that cost ₹52 lakh

children.text: Only the third one changes net worth, because only that one creates profit. This is the link between the two statements: profit earned in the P&L flows into other equity on the balance sheet, less any dividend paid.

body.latex: \text{Closing other equity} = \text{Opening other equity} + \text{Profit for the year} - \text{Dividends}
body.caption: Kesari Foods: ₹13.3 crore + ₹3.7 crore profit - ₹1.0 crore dividend = ₹16.0 crore

body.title: Where the other two statements connect

children.text: The balance sheet is not an island. Three links tie it to everything else you have learned.
To the P&L:
profit for the year increases other equity. Depreciation charged in the P&L reduces the carrying value of property, plant and equipment.
To the cash flow statement:

the cash and cash equivalents line at the bottom of the cash flow statement is exactly the cash line on the balance sheet. The whole statement explains the movement between last year's balance and this year's.
Between two balance sheets:
the change in receivables, inventory and payables from one year to the next is what drives the working capital adjustments in operating cash flow, which you saw in Lesson 1.1.
Lesson 4.3 walks a single transaction through all three statements, so this connection becomes mechanical rather than theoretical.
What the Balance Sheet Does Not Tell You

Assets are generally carried at what they cost, less depreciation, not at what they are worth today. A plot of land bought in 1998 sits at its 1998 price. More importantly, the things that often make an Indian company valuable never appear at all.
Brands built internally:
an acquired brand can appear as an intangible asset, but a brand a company built itself over decades does not.
People and know-how:
your team, its skills and its client relationships are nowhere on the page.
Distribution and reputation:
a network of lakhs of retail outlets is worth a great deal and is recorded at nothing.

Britannia Industries makes the point. Its consolidated balance sheet as at 31 March 2025 shows total assets of ₹8,837 crore and net worth of about ₹4,356 crore, being equity capital of ₹24 crore plus reserves of ₹4,332 crore. The stock market values the company at roughly ₹1.2 lakh crore, about 28 times that net worth. The gap is the brand, the distribution reach and the expected future profits, none of which the balance sheet is designed to capture.

body.text: The reverse trap is just as common. A large asset base is not strength if those assets are slow-moving inventory, receivables from customers who will not pay, or a plant running at 40% utilisation. Lesson 6.2 covers the red flags that separate real assets from decorative ones.

body.title: The ₹2 crore machine request
body.scenario: You head production at Kesari Foods. You want a ₹2 crore automated packing line that will cut packing cost per pack and add capacity. The CFO asks you to explain what it does to the balance sheet before she takes it to the board.
body.prompt: Walk through the effects, and name the two things the CFO will worry about.
body.modelAnswer:
On the day of purchase:
1. Property, plant and equipment rises by ₹2 crore. Nothing hits the P&L yet.
2. The funding side moves too. Paid from cash, the cash line falls by ₹2 crore. Bought on a term loan, borrowings rise by ₹2 crore and debt to equity moves from 0.62 to about 0.72. Bought on supplier credit, trade payables rise until it is paid.
Over the following years:
3. Depreciation, say ₹20 lakh a year over ten years, reduces the asset's carrying value and reduces profit, without any cash leaving the company.
4. If funded by debt, interest appears in finance costs and reduces profit before tax every year.
The two worries:
5. Cash and covenants. A ₹2 crore outflow against a cash balance of ₹1.5 crore means borrowing, and the existing lender may have covenants on debt to equity or interest cover.
6. Utilisation. An asset that runs at half capacity still depreciates fully. The CFO will want the volume assumption behind the saving, not just the saving.
What to bring: the annual cost saving per pack times expected volumes, the payback period, the funding route you propose, and what happens to the numbers if volumes come in 20% below plan.

body.title: Read your own balance sheet
steps: Open the latest balance sheet of your employer or a listed competitor and find total assets and net worth.
Add up all borrowings, long-term and short-term, and divide by net worth to get debt to equity.
Add current assets and divide by current liabilities to get the current ratio.
Find inventories and trade receivables, and compare their total against net worth.
Check how much of total assets is property, plant and equipment, and how much is working capital.
For a listed company, compare market capitalisation with net worth and ask what explains the gap.

cards.definition: Resources the company controls that are expected to bring future benefit.
Obligations to outsiders, from bank loans to supplier dues and employee provisions.
Assets minus liabilities. Share capital plus accumulated retained profits, less dividends.
Assets expected to convert to cash within a year or the operating cycle: inventory, receivables, cash.
Obligations falling due within a year: payables, cash credit, taxes and employee dues.
Long-lived physical assets, carried at cost less accumulated depreciation.
A leased asset capitalised under Ind AS 116, with a matching lease liability.
Reserves, principally retained earnings and securities premium, that sit alongside share capital.

points: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, on every date, at every company.
Assets are what the business uses. Liabilities and equity say who funded them.
Equity, or net worth, is a residual you calculate, not a pool of cash.
Both sides split into current and non-current at roughly the twelve month mark, which is how short-term health is judged.
Every transaction has two effects, and only those that create profit change net worth.
Assets are carried at cost less depreciation, so internally built brands, people and distribution never appear, which is why market value can be many times book value.

body.text: Kesari Foods is fictional and its balance sheet is constructed for teaching. Britannia figures are FY25 consolidated numbers from screener.in, and its market capitalisation changes every trading day. Nothing here is investment advice.
